tier_reason: The allocator source is public (source/) and GCC-8.3.0 plus the Xeon Platinum 8153 CPU are stated. But no optimization flags are given for the benchmarks, and the PARSEC/CORAL-2/Rodinia harness is not in the repo, so it is not A. The work was published peer-reviewed at ISMM 2023 (DOI 10.1145/3591195.3595276, confirmed via Crossref), so it is B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 15.7% faster on average than the second-best allocator (mimalloc-1.6.7) and 20.9% faster than the default Linux allocator (glibc 2.28) across PARSEC, CORAL-2 OpenMP/MPI and real applications. 26.1% faster than glibc on the OpenMP/MPI apps alone. Best case fluidanimate: up to 5.3x faster than glibc, 4.8x faster than TBB and 4.6x faster than mimalloc (ISMM'23 manuscript). The earlier SC'22 draft (SC2022/evaluation.tex) reported 19.0% vs glibc, 6.8x vs Scalloc, and a Rodinia average of 2.44x vs glibc / 2.33x vs mimalloc. The Rodinia claim is commented out of the ISMM'23 manuscript.
corrections.workload: PARSEC (native inputs), five CORAL-2 OpenMP/MPI apps (Nekbone, QMCPACK, LAMMPS, AMG, Quicksilver) and real apps (Apache httpd, MySQL, Memcached, SQLite, Aget, Pfscan, Pbzip2) at 128 threads on an 8-node NUMA machine, plus Hoard synthetic scalability tests (threadtest, larson, cache-scratch, cache-thrash)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC-8.3.0 on Linux Debian 10. The paper gives no optimization flags; the repo's source/Makefile builds the allocator with -g -O2 -std=c++14. Hyperthreading off, transparent huge pages and AutoNUMA enabled, 128 threads (= core count).
corrections.caveats: No top-level LICENSE. Some source files (e.g. libnumalloc.cpp, inherited from FreeGuard) carry GPL-2.0-or-later headers, but most NUMA-specific files (pernodeheap, perthreadheap, interheap) have no license header, so the license is unclear (usability=reference). The repo bundles sources and paper drafts for about 10 UTSASRG projects plus many source-* variant folders, and source/Makefile is configured for NUMA_NODES=2, so which build produced the paper numbers is not obvious. The original benchmark_url was an unpublished SC'22 draft whose numbers differ from the later ISMM'23 manuscript (19.0% vs 20.9% over glibc; Rodinia claim dropped). The draft also contradicts itself on fluidanimate (5.3x vs 2.9x over glibc). Last push 2023-03-01 (>3 years ago): abandoned.

notes: The numbers in the original record do appear verbatim in SC2022/evaluation.tex, but that is a pre-publication draft. The peer-reviewed venue is ISMM 2023, so benchmark_url and claimed_speedup were re-pointed to the ISMM2023 manuscript in the repo; the published ACM text itself was not opened. Downgraded from A to B because the paper states no compile flags and the repo has no benchmark harness.

tier_reason: The ISMM'15 paper source states gcc 4.8.3 / glibc 2.18 / Fedora 20 and the CPUs (i7-4770, Xeon E5-2665). The benchmark code is public in the same repo (tests/new-malloc-test.c, with raw data in paper/ismm15/*.data), and release/Makefile sets -O3 -flto (-mrtm for HTM). That meets A.

corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 (Haswell-DT, 4 cores / 8 HW threads, 3.4GHz, 1 socket) for the HTM results; 2-socket 16-core Intel Xeon E5-2665 (Sandy Bridge, 2.4GHz, 32 HW threads) for the non-HTM 32-thread results
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.3 on Linux 3.15.7 / glibc 2.18 (Fedora 20), per the paper. Release build flags -O3 -flto -pthread -fPIC, plus -mrtm for the HTM build (release/Makefile, Makefile.include). Compared against Hoard 3.10, jemalloc 3.6.0, tbb43_20140724 and DLmalloc 2.8.6.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark toolchain (gcc 4.8.3 / glibc 2.18 / Fedora 20) is from 2015. The last commit on any branch is 2017-10-25 (GitHub pushed_at of 2019-11-15 has no matching commit), and there is no recent head-to-head vs mimalloc/snmalloc/rpmalloc. The numbers come from the author's own malloc-test variant in the ISMM'15 paper. The paper's 'DLmalloc' is standalone Doug Lea dlmalloc 2.8.6 linked separately, not glibc's ptmalloc2-based default malloc, so glibc malloc itself was not measured. The fastest path relies on Haswell TSX/HTM; a pthread-mutex build also exists. Dual-licensed: MIT (expat) or GPLv3-or-later.

notes: The abstract states 2.1x / 2.75x / 3.4x over the best of DLmalloc/JEmalloc/Hoard/TBBmalloc verbatim. Metadata fixes: the license is MIT OR GPL-3.0-or-later (the GPL text says 'or any later version'), and last_commit is 2017-10-25, not 2019-11-15. compared_against_cpp_std_directly is set to false because the 'DLmalloc' baseline is standalone dlmalloc 2.8.6, not the system glibc malloc.

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed OOPSLA'15 paper (Artifact Evaluated) comparing against ptmalloc2 on SPEC 483.xalancbmk and threadtest/shbench/larson/ACDC, with hardware (4x Xeon E7-4850) stated. Neither the paper nor the artifact README (only 'tested on Ubuntu 14.04') gives the compiler or flags, so it is B, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: About 1.28x SPEC ratio vs ptmalloc2 on single-threaded 483.xalancbmk (read from the Figure 5 bar chart, derived from page data). Here scalloc is mid-pack, below TCMalloc (~1.345), llalloc (~1.33), TBB (~1.29) and SuperMalloc (~1.285), and the paper says the differences among the best allocators are small. For multithreaded workloads the paper claims scalloc 'increases performance on average while consuming less memory than the previously fastest allocator (TBB)' and outperforms/outscales all allocators for varying object sizes that fit virtual spans.
corrections.caveats: The OOPSLA'15 paper (arXiv v2, Aug 2015) is 10+ years old. The current README says the allocator was 'completely rewritten from scratch' since the paper and says to benchmark the current version; the separate cksystemsgroup/scalloc-artifact repo was last updated 2018-03-20. Today's numbers may therefore differ from the paper's. The paper states no compiler or optimization flags. The xalancbmk values exist only as bars in Figure 5, not as printed numbers.

notes: The record's '~1.33x, on par with TCMalloc ~1.34x' misread Figure 5: the ~1.33 bar is llalloc, and scalloc's bar is about 1.28. claimed_speedup was corrected and verdict downgraded (tier stays B). The 'artifact not updated since 2019' caveat was corrected to 2018-03-20.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C to A. The benchmark code is public (benchmarks/bench.cpp, Google Benchmark, arena vs malloc/free), and CMakeLists.txt pins the compiler to g++-14 with Release flags -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -DNDEBUG. The README names the CPUs (AMD EPYC 7763; Apple M1 under OrbStack). The >50x cap does not apply because flags are stated.

corrections.baseline: malloc/free (system C allocator; the benchmark calls malloc/free directly, not operator new/delete)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++-14 (hard-coded via CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER in CMakeLists.txt; exact minor version not stated), C++23, Release: -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -Wall -Wextra -Werror -DNDEBUG
corrections.workload: Google Benchmark: allocate N (1-1024) 64-byte objects then release them in bulk (arena reset() vs N free() calls, both inside the timed loop), plus a mixed 8/64/256-byte alloc+release batch
corrections.caveats: Very new (last commit 2026-07-21), 1-star personal project, not peer reviewed. EPYC 7763 numbers come from a shared GitHub Codespaces VM. The largest multiples (97x-342x on Apple M1) were measured under OrbStack virtualization, which the README itself calls not native hardware; the malloc side there may be a non-glibc libc. The workload favors a bump allocator by construction: the arena releases everything with one O(1) reset while malloc pays N individual frees, and the arena has no per-object free.

notes: All README numbers match the record (10x-27x and 15x on EPYC; 32x-342x and 15x on M1). The tier is upgraded to A because the compiler (g++-14) is pinned in CMakeLists.txt and flags plus CPU are stated. If the pipeline requires the compiler to be named on the results page itself, it drops back to C.

tier_reason: The arXiv preprint ('Manuscript submitted to ACM', v1 only) states 1.75x/1.18x/1.15x/1.23x/1.18x over jemalloc/TCMalloc/mimalloc/Mallacc/Memento, with a stated gem5 setup and GCC 9.4 -O3. It is not peer reviewed and has no public code, so it is C.

corrections.workload: gem5 full-system simulation of 10 multithreaded workloads: 7 from mimalloc-bench (larson, xmalloc, cache-scratch, sh6bench/sh8bench, mstress, alloctest), GAPBS BFS and BC (64k-node synthetic graph), and NAS DC. Also single-threaded espresso/cfrac and 6 Redis-benchmark ops.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.4, -O3, -march=armv8.1-a (for far atomics), used for SpeedMalloc and all workloads
corrections.hardware: Simulated only (gem5 full system): 1-16 AArch64 out-of-order big cores (32KB L1d/L1i, 256KB L2, 2MB LLC per core) plus 1 in-order AArch64 support core (16KB L1d/L1i) and 16GB DDR4-2400. No real silicon or FPGA prototype.
corrections.caveats: arXiv preprint (Aug 2025, v1, 'Manuscript submitted to ACM'), with no linked code or artifact. SpeedMalloc is a hardware proposal: a dedicated support core on the coherent bus that the authors say needs ISA and hardware not present in current systems. It is a research reference, not a deployable library, and all results come from gem5 simulation. It compares only against jemalloc, TCMalloc, mimalloc, Mallacc and Memento, never against glibc malloc or std::allocator.

notes: The numbers match the abstract and body. The main correction is that this is a simulated hardware design (gem5, AArch64), not software, so it belongs in the research-only section. hardware and compiler fields were filled from the paper's section 6.1.
